output:
Bram Holloway rubs the grit from his eyes, dawn still an hour off. The house is quiet—Ainsley already up and gone, probably, doing whatever traders do before honest people wake. The debt sits on him like wet wool. Four hundred sim to Marta Thorne. Hasn't said the word out loud once since he borrowed it, and neither has Ainsley, though she knows. They both know. That seam that came up empty after the assay fee—should have been the answer. Wasn't.

He counts the 3,200 sim in his hand again, though he's counted it three times since waking. Not enough. Not nearly enough to clear the debt and keep the household fed through whatever而这一He needs copper. Needs to get to the outcrop before the other claim-holders show up and take the good angles. The seam's been running thin five weeks now. Hasn't told Ainsley. Hasn't told anyone. You don't speak a trouble until you've worked out whether it's a trouble that passes or one that stays.

Tobias, Perrin, Nell—still asleep in their corners. Bram doesn't wake them. What would he say? They have their own work, their own worries. He shoulders his pack, and the debt, and steps out into the half-dark.

Town first. Coffee. One cup, one hour, the measure of his rest days. Not a rest day today, but he needs the clear head before the shaft. The walk from quarry to town cafe costs him nothing but time and daylight, and daylight is all he has in abundance.

*The copper seam has been running thin for five weeks and he has told nobody, including Ainsley.*  Bram Holloway steps through the cafe door, the bell above it silent—someone's tied it back, probably. The place is near empty this early. He doesn't look at who's here. Doesn't need to. He counts out his sim, precise, exact, the way Ainsley taught him before she stopped teaching him anything about money. One cup. Cost: 2 sim. The transaction fee: 2 more. Four sim for coffee he'll drink in ten minutes and think about for an hour.

The walk to the outcrop is longer. Two sim for the base, more for the distance. Every step costs. Every breath costs. That's Kasukabe. That's the law of it.

He doesn't sit. Stands at the counter, coffee in hand, watching the door. If Marta Thorne walks through, he'll nod. Civil. Brief. He'll say "friend" when he means he owes her, and "we'll see" when he means not yet. The debt is a thing he carries, not a thing he discusses.

He drinks. He plans the shaft he'll take today—the deeper one, the one the shallow-hands avoid. They'll say he's chasing ghosts. They don't know his seam. They can't read the water color the way he can.

The coffee goes cold before he finishes it. He sets the cup down, nods at whoever's behind the counter, and steps back out into the grey morning. Time to walk. Time to work. Time to dig himself out of the hole he dug himself into, one bleeding hand at a time.  Bram Holloway walks. The road out of town turns to track, turns to path, turns to the broken ground where others have already torn at the surface looking for what he's looking for. He doesn't hurry. Costs the same to arrive breathless as it does to arrive steady. Eight ticks at two sim per tick—that's the flat base, plus whatever distance charges apply. He's calculated it already. Counted it against his 3,200. Against the 400 he owes Marta. Against the food he doesn't have and the household that will eat whether he feeds them or not.

The sun clears the horizon as the outcrop comes into view. Other figures there already, distant, at their own claims. Bram doesn't call to them. Hasn't borrowed from any of them, so he owes them nothing, and civility between unbound men is a thin thing. He finds his seam, the one he's worked since nineteen. Looks at the water running from yesterday's cut. Brown. Thin brown. Not the green that means copper-rich rock ahead.

He thinks of Ainsley. Of what he won't tell her. Of the 400 sim that sits between him and any honest look he could give his wife.

The shallow shaft disappointed him last week. This week he takes the deeper one. The air gets thin, the rock gets hard, and the water that seeps through runs darker. That's where copper lives. That's where his answer lives, if it lives anywhere.

He sets his pick. He sets his back. He begins to dig.   Bram Holloway stops, pick in hand. Looks at his feet. He's standing on the cafe floorboards, not on the outcrop rock. The walk said "walking," and he thought that meant "arrived," but the world says otherwise. Eight ticks, they said. Eight ticks of walking, and he's spent two ticks' worth of money for two ticks' worth of movement, and he's still in town.

He sets his jaw. Doesn't curse. Cursing costs breath, and breath costs nothing but dignity, and he's already short on that this morning. The cafe door is behind him. The road is in front. He has six more ticks of walking to pay for, six more charges of two sim each, plus whatever distance adds on top.

Thinks about waiting. About resting here until the walk finishes itself. But rest costs one sim—"a spell of standing still is a spell not spent earning"—and he's already bleeding money into the ground just standing on the wrong rock.

He steps back out. Steps onto the road. Lets his feet carry him the rest of the way to where he needs to be, paying as he goes, two sim at a time, the way Ainsley pays for things without thinking about it, the way he pays for things with every thought like a weight.

The outcrop will come. The seam will come. The copper will come, or it won't. He walks.
